newsitem.title: UK: Former British minister says took lobbyist's cash.
newsitem.headline: Former British minister says took lobbyist's cash.

text.p: A former Conservative minister who has vowed to clear his name of sleaze allegations on Wednesday admitted he took money from a parliamentary lobbyist, but said he did not believe he had entered any financial arrangement.

Neil Hamilton pulled out of what had been billed as the "libel trial of the century" against the Guardian newspaper late on Monday, only hours before it was due to start. He continued to deny the newspaper's claims that he had accepted cash in exchange for asking questions in parliament.
But Hamilton told a BBC television interviewer that he had accepted two payments totalling 10,000 pounds ($15,660) from parliamentary lobbyist Ian Greer in the late 1980s.
"It was very fraught circumstances. The conversation we had was in terms of a kind of retainer relationship or consultancy agreement with Greer to do with things in Parliament," said Hamilton.
"I didn't consider I had any financial relationship with Ian Greer," he said.
Hamilton, a member of the ruling Conservative Party, said the payments were made in exchange for introducing a client to the lobbyist.

Prime Minister John Major and his deputy Michael Heseltine had both been subpoenaed to testify in the case, which was expected to revive a reputation for sleaze which has dogged the ruling Conservative Party for the past few years.
Sixteen Conservative members of parliament have been forced to resign from posts since 1992 because of sleaze allegations.

Hamilton was forced to resign as trade minister in October 1994 after the Guardian accused him of accepting money from Mohammed al-Fayed, the Egyptian-born owner of London's luxury Harrods store, in return for tabling questions in parliament.
On Tuesday the Guardian named four other senior Conservatives who it said were involved in a paid campaign to promote the interests of the Harrods boss.

The newspaper's Wednesday edition published the names of 21 members of parliament from Britain's three main parties it said had accepted money from Greer, saying its information came from a Conservative Party memorandum.
Greer had also planned to sue the Guardian for libel, but he pulled out of the trial along with Hamilton.
The timing of the reports is particularly unwelcome for the Conservative Party because it is due next week to hold its last annual conference before the next general election.
The opposition Labour Party's own conference, underway this week, has already been hailed as a success following a stirring speech by leader Tony Blair.

Judge Lord Michael Nolan, who chaired a commission into standards in public life called by Major to limit the political damage of the sleaze allegations, has called for the allegations to be "investigated without delay".
"The continuing accusations and counter-accusations in this case are damaging to the reputation of parliament, and the truth of the matter needs to be properly investigated," he said.
